title: Habits, Change & Small Challenges
subtitle: Review habit-change language, clear routines, and the idea of a manageable challenge.

sections.label: Lesson Notes
sections.title: What we explored
sections.intro: This lesson focused on habits, personal routines, and the idea that a small, repeated challenge can support change.

cards.title: A habit is repeated behaviour
cards.text: A habit can be helpful or unhelpful. Change begins by noticing what you do regularly and choosing one realistic action.

cards.title: Small and specific works best
cards.text: Instead of trying to change everything at once, choose one action you can repeat. Notice what makes it easier or harder.

cards.title: Talk about routines clearly
cards.text: Use present simple for usual routines: “I usually walk to work.” Add frequency words such as usually, often, sometimes, and rarely.

sections.label: Grammar
sections.title: Present simple for routines
sections.intro: Use the present simple to describe habits, routines, and things that are generally true.

cards.title: Form
cards.text: I/you/we/they walk. He/she walks. Use do/does for questions and do not/does not for negatives.

cards.title: Frequency words
cards.text: Place usually, often, sometimes, and rarely before the main verb: “She often listens to music.” With be, place them after be: “They are usually tired.”

cards.title: A useful question
cards.text: Ask: Is this a repeated routine or a fact? If yes, present simple is usually the right starting point.

cards.title: challenge yourself
cards.text: try to do something difficult in order to improve

cards.title: build a habit
cards.text: make a useful action part of your routine

cards.title: routine
cards.text: the things you usually do in a regular order

cards.title: manageable
cards.text: possible to do without becoming overwhelming

cards.title: opportunity
cards.text: a chance to do something useful or positive

questions.q: Choose the best sentence for a regular routine.
opt: I am usually walk to work.
questions.hint: Use the base verb after I.
Think about making something less frequent.

questions.q: Complete: She ___ checks her phone before bed.
questions.hint: Put the frequency word before the main verb.

readings.title: Making a Routine More Manageable
readings.text:
A new habit often begins with a large idea: exercise more, read more, sleep earlier, or spend less time on a phone. The idea can be useful, but it may feel too big. When a goal is unclear, it is difficult to know what to do on an ordinary busy day. A manageable challenge is more specific. For example, a person might decide to read for ten minutes after dinner, prepare clothes for the morning, or take a short walk three times a week.

The first days are not always easy. A routine can be interrupted by work, tiredness, visitors, or a change of plan. This does not mean the challenge has failed. It is more useful to notice the problem and return to the action when possible. A habit becomes stronger through repetition, not through one perfect week.

It also helps to connect a new action to something that already happens. Someone who makes tea every evening can put a book beside the cup. Someone who uses public transport can listen to a short English audio during the journey. The action becomes easier to remember because it has a place in the day.

Finally, a challenge should feel personal. Two people may want different changes, and that is normal. The important question is not “What is the biggest challenge?” but “What small action can I repeat?” A realistic plan gives a person an opportunity to practise, adjust, and notice progress.

questions.q: Why can a large goal be difficult?
opt: It gives no clear action for a busy day.
It always takes only ten minutes.

questions.q: What should a learner do after an interrupted routine?
opt: Notice the problem and return when possible.

questions.q: What is one way to remember a new action?
opt: Connect it to something you already do.
Only do it on perfect days.

sections.label: Listening
sections.title: Listening follow-up
sections.intro: The lesson included listening connected to habit change. Use this short follow-up after you hear an English song, podcast clip, or video about changing routines.

cards.title: First listen
cards.text: Listen once for the main idea. Is the speaker describing a habit to start, stop, or change?

cards.title: Second listen
cards.text: Write three words or short phrases you notice. Then make one present-simple sentence with one of them.

cards.title: Keep it light
cards.text: You do not need to understand every word. Aim to catch the message and one useful phrase.

questions.q: Which sentence describes a usual routine?
opt: I usually go to bed before midnight.
I am usually go to bed before midnight.
I usually going to bed before midnight.
I go usually to bed before midnight.

questions.q: Which word means “possible to do without too much difficulty”?
Complete: He ___ to reduce screen time this month.

questions.hint: It is about ending an unhelpful routine.

questions.q: Choose the best frequency word: I ___ read on the train, but not every day.
questions.hint: The sentence is about how often.

questions.q: What does the reading recommend after a missed day?
opt: Return to the action when you can.
She often listens to English audio.
She often listen to English audio.
She is often listen to English audio.
She listening often to English audio.

questions.q: A challenge can become easier to remember when you…
opt: connect it to an existing routine
questions.hint: Use an action you already do as a cue.

questions.q: Which phrase means “try to improve by doing something difficult”?
What is the main message of this package?
opt: Small repeated actions can support change.
